# UPDATE: Pony.ai Deep Dive

**From:** The AV Market Strategist <avmarketstrategist@substack.com>  
**Date:** 2026-09-03T09:10:11.000Z

---

👋 Hey everyone,
Pony.ai reported Q2 2026 on August 18. Nine days later I finished rebuilding the living deep dive around it.
Then, on August 25, the company filed something that changed one of the sections I had already written. More on that below.
If you have not come across these before: the deep dives are the long-form company files I keep current, so there is one document that is actually up to date instead of a pile of old posts. WeRide came first, Pony.ai is the second, and the AV fleet operations file followed. I update them whenever there is a material event.
What I changed this time
The full Q2 and first-half financials, rebuilt. Revenue, margin, the operating expense line that changed the story, and the cash position. Q2 is the first quarter where the operating model shows up in the accounts rather than in the narrative. One number underneath the headline moved in the opposite direction, and it is the one I would build a model on.
New section: what the 691% is actually made of. Robotaxi revenue grew almost eightfold. It is also three different kinds of revenue stacked into one reported line, and they are not worth the same. Pony’s own reporting gives you the tool to separate them. The split is close to even, and the half that gets the attention is not the half that compounds.
New section: the Sinotrans relationship. Pony’s largest customer is also its joint venture partner and, as of two days ago, its export logistics provider. Three roles, one counterparty. A Hong Kong filing published after trading hours on August 25 puts hard numbers on how big that relationship is contracted to become through early 2028, and one of them is larger than Pony’s entire group revenue in 2025. I have not seen it covered anywhere. It also quietly dates the month Pony started shipping vehicles out of China.
A correction to my own forecast. I wrote in an earlier version that the trucking fleet could exit 2026 above a thousand vehicles. Pony has since published its own timetable and that call was roughly two years early. The corrected numbers are in the file, along with a light-truck target an order of magnitude larger than anything I had modelled, and the executive’s own explanation for the delay, which is a cost statement rather than a technology one.
The arithmetic behind the two full-year targets. Both were raised in May and restated in August. Both are now testable against the half-year print. Both require a step change rather than a continuation, and the most likely path to hitting one of them runs straight through the revenue that does not compound.
The Middle East, reframed. Still one of the largest near-term opportunities in this thesis. No longer one where Pony arrives first. Two Chinese competitors are already running driverless commercial service on Uber in the same two Dubai neighbourhoods where Pony has yet to launch, and that changes what the competitive question in the Gulf actually is.
Korea, signed on August 28. A 200-vehicle commercial commitment with a KOSDAQ-listed partner, a certification gate that has to clear before it converts, and the clearest public statement Pony has made about where data collected overseas is stored. It lines up almost word for word with something Bolt told me on the podcast, which is the part I found interesting.
Europe, all three entry vectors current. Zagreb live on the Uber app, the 2,000-vehicle agreement across five cities, and the Bolt and Stellantis programme that has moved from announcement to operating pilot. Including the one qualification about Zagreb that most coverage left out.
The asset-light claim, checked against the accounts. Management guided that nearly half of 2026’s new vehicles would be partner-funded. That figure has not been repeated in either 2026 quarter, and capital expenditure is moving the other way. WeRide’s CEO told me on Autonomy Insiders why the domestic half of this model is the harder half, and I think the same constraint applies here.
Fleet, footprint, unit economics and risks, all current. Including one metric that has now gone five quarters without being restated, which would matter less if it were not one of the three legs holding up the unit-economics story.
The weekly newsletter is free, and it stays free.
The deep dives are the part I keep for the readers who chose to support this work when they did not have to. If you are on the free list, this is exactly what a paid subscription funds: every living company file kept current, the full financial breakdowns, and the analysis behind the numbers.
If you already support The AV Market Strategist, thank you. The updated file is live now.
Thanks for reading.
Daniel
